summary: Questions for both sides, each pressing the premise with the thinnest evidence or the broadest reach.

points.title: For S1 -- the productivity premise (n2)
points.text: What shows that people are more productive when they control their environment -- productive at which tasks, and measured how? This probes n2, the broadest premise of the case, because it asserts a gain without any task or measure.

points.title: For S1 -- fewer interruptions mean more output (n3)
points.text: Do fewer interruptions at home mean more output for every kind of work, or only for focused solo tasks that need little feedback? This probes n3, which stretches a finding about focused tasks onto all output.

points.title: For S2 -- informal chats as problem solving (n4)
points.text: How much real problem solving happens in informal office conversations, and could a remote team keep that with scheduled collaboration? This probes n4, which treats the office habit as the only source of a real good.

points.title: For S2 -- the companies you know (n6)
points.text: You know a handful of companies that brought people back -- what of the companies you do not know, and might leases or roles explain the pattern? This probes n6, which generalizes from a small sample to all companies.

points.title: For S2 -- junior onboarding slower remotely (n8)
points.text: Is remote onboarding slower because it is remote, or because onboarding was never structured -- what would a fair comparison measure? This probes n8, the strongest objection, because it still assumes the cause without comparing like with like.
